title: Emergency Prices: How Private Equity Captured the Ambulance Market
author: Matt Stoller
content:
_Dan Geller is a Staff Attorney at Antimonopoly Counsel and can be reached at
dan@antimonopoly.us._

In 2023, the city of Evanston, Illinois
[raised](https://cityofevanston.civicweb.net/document/267844/Ordinance%20103-O-23,%20Amending%20Title%209,%20Chapter%202.pdf?handle=A3F648D1E227482BA5BAEB75A93A0499#:~:text=Page%205,dollars;%20and)
its ambulance fee from $1500 to $2000, with a $15 mileage charge tacked on.
Like many municipalities, city officials and taxpayers have gotten used to
ever-increasing prices for basic services, all bucketed under the "cost of
living" crisis we're dealing with. In fact, yesterday the Michigan University
consumer sentiment indicator [hit the worst
reading](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/10/consumer-sentiment-inflation-fears-
iran-war.html) it has ever recorded, going all the way back to 1961. The
endless increases in prices for all sorts of random necessities is a key
reason.

But these cost hikes don't just 'happen,' as if it's some sort of natural
event. Markets are a function of law. There are companies and dealers and
financiers behind every industry, so we can actually try to understand why
they are happening. In this case, Evanston chalked up the hike to, among other
things, the increasing of "cost of equipment and vehicles used for emergency
responses." The ambulance market, once a decentralized set of family owned
firms, has been rolled up into a consolidated industry run by private equity.
And the price hikes followed.

This story isn't unusual. In early 2025, BIG
[traced](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/did-a-private-equity-fire-truck-
roll) a roll-up of fire trucks and fire apparatus, leading to a crisis in that
sector. It turns out that something similar seems to have happened here, with
some of the same players.

Let's go back to Evanston. In 2011, the city purchased an ambulance for
[$148,000](https://evanstonnow.com/new-ambulance-to-cost-
nearly-500k/#:~:text=John%20M,%2C%20if%20not%2C%20why%20not?), an
International MedTec used as a reserve vehicle to back up the rest of its
fleet. The average ambulance is designed to last [5-7
years](https://www.cvfrs.com/post/ambulance-replacement-faq) based on normal
wear and tear. "Emergency response miles are a lot harder on a vehicle than
routine traveling to work miles," said one [fire
chief](https://www.metrowestdailynews.com/story/news/2007/06/26/natick-
purchases-new-
ambulance/41319252007/#:~:text=Natick%20purchases%20new%20ambulance,town's%20ambulance%20service%2C%20he%20said.).
But Evanston kept this one for more than 13 years, spending as much as the
original purchase price on repairs to keep it going. In 2024, Evanston finally
buckled down and got a new one for half a million dollars. In thirteen years,
the price increased by 337% -- 297% above inflation. And these vehicles are
often on long backorders; in the case of Evanston, the ambulance they ordered
"won't be delivered for at least two years because of production backups."

In 2025, North Olmsted in Ohio had a [similar
experience](https://www.cleveland.com/community/2025/10/north-olmsted-fire-
department-set-to-purchase-new-495000-ambulance.html).

> City Council is expected to approve the North Olmsted Fire Department's
> request to purchase a new $495,000 ambulance…
>
> The expenditure -- which is coming out of the general fund -- marks quite an
> increase since the fire department's 2021 ambulance purchase price of
> $353,000.
>
> "We're seeing that across the board with not just med units but all kinds of
> fire equipment," he said.
>
> That's not the only bad news associated with the new ambulance purchase.
>
> "They're telling us delivery ETA is 925 to 950 days from the date of order,"
> he said. "Our lead times are long now, quite a ways out. That would be 2028,
> so it's gonna be a while.
>
> "The days are gone when you could just call up a manufacturer and say you
> need one by the end of the year. That doesn't happen anymore."

We at BIG have tracked ambulance prices as best we can through public news
reports, and have found that the experience of these two cities tracks the
overall trend.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3vx1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4b310c88-0e61-4aac-875b-70b56d2a3238_693x521.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3vx1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4b310c88-0e61-4aac-875b-70b56d2a3238_693x521.png)Ambulance
pricing from public sources listed
[here](https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/z4aareh1kfdjo9mei3b4m/Ambulance-cost-
examples-1999-2025.pdf?rlkey=6dp2lz6gqkab3wedvk0f9q97d&e=1&dl=0).

We have been trying to understand why these delays and price hikes are
happening. We spoke with Ellen Dayan, who negotiates contracts for cities at
the Suburban Purchasing Cooperative. And she told us the price for a base
Horton ambulance just went up in July of last year, from $397,595 to $464,198.
When I asked why, she referred me to a Horton dealer, who then referred us to
a spokesperson for a private equity conglomerate, REV Group, which owns Horton
and 13 other brands. That spokesperson did not respond to our questions,
though the [company's most recent investor
material](https://investors.revgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/Rev-IR/reports-and-
presentations/4q25-earning-slides.pdf) does mention "increased … pricing of
ambulances" and "higher … price realization" as significant factors behind
growing revenue and profits.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ckxY!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3a723816-eb98-4acc-9b89-484ff2765752_788x425.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ckxY!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3a723816-eb98-4acc-9b89-484ff2765752_788x425.png)

"25 years of EMS and ambulance designs are stagnant," said [one
commenter](https://www.reddit.com/r/ems/comments/1lfvstb/comment/myvfhsf/) in
an EMS channel on Reddit. "Most manufacturers are like: 'We added a shelf for
a monitor' 'We added a harness to the bench' 'We added LED cabinet lighting'
That will be $300k please!"

Emergency vehicles have always been more expensive than ordinary cars, because
manufacturers must combine a truck-like chassis that can move quickly, with a
platform to provide pre-hospital emergency care. Ambulances contain an HVAC
system, oxygen delivery and suction services, electrical and electronic
medical devices, a communications platform, and so forth. They are complex,
they crash a lot, and they are packed with technology.

Like most areas of the economy, the post-pandemic era caused problems in the
supply chain. Moreover, we are an aging society, so there is increasing
ambulance demand in North America, where orders have grown from an estimated
6300 per year in [2017](https://investors.revgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/Rev-
IR/Annual%20Reports/rev-annual-report-2017.pdf), to 8500 in
[2022](https://www.ems1.com/ems-products/fleet-management/articles/when-the-
chips-are-down-ambulance-chassis-availability-now-at-crisis-levels-
fdggdvlHfQ9c5uTw/). Experts see the space growing by ten percent annually
through [2030](https://www.wfmynews2.com/article/money/updated-ambulance-
vehicles-driving-around-guilford-county-commission-ems-ambulance-box-
chassis/83-0c07d1de-d672-463d-b8bc-3c3ce70a074d). The industry has blamed its
inability to keep pace with rising demand on [essential microchip
shortages](https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/global-microchip-shortage-
impacting-ambulance-
supply/story?id=77827044#:~:text=MORE:%20Semiconductor%20shortage%20puts%20the,%2C%202021%2C%20in%20New%20York.&text=He%20said%20it%20takes%20between,likely%20in%20the%20near%20future.%22),
[chassis production halts](https://ambulance.org/2021/05/19/microchip-
shortage-to-affect-ambulance-supply/) leading to a 1.1 million unit shortfall
in 2021, [tariffs ,](https://www.sootoday.com/local-news/trumps-tariffs-could-
drive-up-ambulance-costs-by-10-say-
manufacturers-10404241#:~:text=Trump's%20tariffs%20could%20drive%20up,that%20supplies%20its%20emergency%20lights.)
[labor shortages](https://www.scmr.com/article/labor-shortages-remain-an-
ongoing-concern-in-many-parts-of-u.s-manufacturing) in the manufacturing
sector, and [low unemployment rates](https://www.fanucamerica.com/case-
studies/life-line-
graymatter#:~:text=Emergency%20Vehicle%20Maker%20Tackles%20Labor%20Shortage%20and%20Enhances%20Efficiency%20through,to%20address%20time%2Dsensitive%20tasks)
making it difficult to find reliable labor.

But there's also been a change in the market structure. The industry was once
defined by relatively stable costs--for example, Winter Springs, Florida paid
$135,000 per ambulance in
[2000,](https://weblink.winterspringsfl.org/WebLink/DocView.aspx?id=382166&dbid=0&repo=WinterSprings&cr=1___.YzJ1OmFlbHBlY29ub21pY2xpYmVydGllczpjOm86M2YyNGQwZGMwNTE2M2ZlNGZhOWRmNzRhYWI3MjBlMDc6NzoxNzlmOjZjMjI4ZjgyODQ3MjZkZjRiMjhhNTg3NGZlN2Y5ZTc0NDA0YzMxYjkyZWIwY2FjNTQ0ODk1ZDZmYmQ1MDUwZDg6cDpUOkY)
while Natick, Massachusetts paid $132,600 for a new ambulance in 2007, often
delivered within a [120-day window](https://naemt.org/docs/default-
source/advocacy-documents/letters-and-comments/final--dot-ambulance-shortage-
lettere31e9133fe31667a9799ff0000a338da.pdf#:~:text=Lead%20times%20for%20new%20ambulance%20deliveries%20have,is%20the%20most%20crippling%20of%20the%20shortages.).

### The Roll-Up

Behind this pricing model was a competitive industry, comprised of family-
owned and privately held companies serving specific regions. Major companies
included [Wheeled Coach](https://wheeledcoach.com/about/) (founded in Florida
in 1975), [American Emergency Vehicles](https://emergency-medical-
service.fandom.com/wiki/American_Emergency_Vehicles) (AEV) (founded in North
Carolina in 1982), [Horton
Ambulance](https://fire.fandom.com/wiki/Horton_Emergency_Vehicles) (founded in
Ohio in 1968), [Leader Ambulance ](https://midvalleynews.com/leader-emergency-
vehicles-
marks-50-years/#:~:text=Leader%20Emergency%20Vehicles%20opened%20its,that%20defined%20its%20first%20decade.)(founded
in California in 1975), [Road Rescue
](https://roadrescue.com/about/#:~:text=Today,reduced%20labor%20without%20impacting%20safety.)(founded
in Minnesota in 1976), [Braun Ambulance](https://www.braunambulances.com/us-
ohio-ambulance-manufacturer/) (founded in Ohio in 1961), [Mccoy Miller
Emergency
Vehicles](https://fire.fandom.com/wiki/McCoy_Miller_Emergency_Vehicles)
(founded in Indiana in 1974), and [Marque
Ambulance](https://fire.fandom.com/wiki/Marque_Ambulance) (founded in Indiana
in 1990).

The story of how a once vibrant industry turned brittle begins in the
mid-2000s, when a private equity firm named American Industrial Partners (AIP)
decided to enter the business and consolidate the makers of modular
ambulances. AIP specializes in "middle market" industrial businesses; it is
already being [investigated by the Senate
](https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/subcommittees/dmdcc/hearings/sounding-the-
alarm-americas-fire-apparatus-crisis/)and Federal antitrust enforcers for its
roll-up of fire trucks and fire apparatuses, which caused price hikes and
shortages in that sector. And its work in ambulances seems to mirror its fire
apparatus approach.

In 2006, AIP [acquired](https://busride.com/rev-group-sets-itself-
apart/#:~:text=The%20evolution%20of%20REV,Spartan%20Motors%20\(September%202010\).)
ambulance manufacturer Wheeled Coach, an iconic Florida firm that made
ambulances for cities all over the world, as well as the military, the FBI and
the Secret Service. "Anywhere the president of the United States goes, there's
a Wheeled Coach ambulance following him," said Wheeled Coach head of sales
[Paul Holzapfel](https://www.fireapparatusmagazine.com/fire-
apparatus/ambulances/wheeled-coach-celebrates-50-years-of-serving-communities-
ambulance-needs/). This acquisition marked the first step in a dramatic
restructuring of the industry.

A few years after buying Wheeled Coach, AIP [acquired Halcore
Group](https://americanindustrial.com/american-industrial-partners-purchases-
halcore-group-inc/), the parent company of Horton Ambulance, American
Emergency Vehicles, and Leader Ambulance, which were "some of the longest
standing and most respected brand names in the emergency vehicle market," with
production facilities in Ohio, North Carolina and California. That same year,
AIP [acquired modular ambulance producer Road
Rescue](https://americanindustrial.com/allied-specialty-vehicles-inc-
announces-the-acquisition-of-road-rescue/) from Spartan Motors, Inc. (and
eventually acquired Spartan in [2020](https://investors.revgroup.com/investor-
releases/2020/02-03-2020-135942281)). Around 2015, AIP bundled all of the
companies it acquired in the specialty-vehicle sector into a conglomerate
called REV Group, which it took public in 2017. AIP retained control over REV
Group until 2024, when it took advantage of REV Group's skyrocketing stock
price to sell most of its shares. Finally, last year, REV Group
[sold](https://revgroup.com/terex-and-rev-group-complete-merger-creating-a-
premier-specialty-equipment-manufacturer/) itself to another public company
that makes specialty vehicles and various equipment for them, Terex.

The level of concentration is high, though we can't get exact numbers. In
2017, REV Group told investors it controlled [forty-four
percent](https://investors.revgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/Rev-
IR/Annual%20Reports/rev-annual-report-2017#page=18.pdf) of the North American
ambulance manufacturing market. Seven years later, Mike Virnig, the head of
REV Group's Specialty Vehicles division, went on the show [Jay Leno's
Garage](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GPcacmetIX4&t=85s) to talk to the
famous comedian about the company's new electric line of vehicles. He noted
the company's ambulance manufacturing market share is closer to seventy
percent.

A different private equity firm engineered the consolidation of the remainder
of the market. In [2004](https://www.demers-ambulances.com/ca-en/about-
us/demers-ambulance-manufacturing-history/#development), Canadian private
equity firm Novacap acquired the previously independent Demers Ambulance
Manufacturer (Demers), one of the largest ambulance manufacturers in North
America. In 2012, Westerkirk Capital Partners and Ironbridge Equity Partners
[acquired ](https://ironbridgeequity.com/2012/08/06/westerkirk-capital-and-
ironbridge-equity-partners-announces-that-they-together-with-management-have-
acquired-demers-ambulance-manufacturer-inc-demers-ambulances/)Demers from
Novacap before selling Demers to Clearspring Capital Partners [in
2016](https://ironbridgeequity.com/2016/11/23/ironbridge-equity-partners-
enters-agreement-to-sell-demers-ambulances/).

Clearspring then acquired [Braun Ambulance ](https://www.demers-
ambulances.com/press_release/leading-ambulance-manufacturers-braun-industries-
demers-ambulances-joining-forces/)and [Crestline
Coach](https://www.pehub.com/clearspring-backed-demers-braun-acquires-
crestline-coach/) in 2018, followed by [Medix Specialty
Vehicles](https://www.lfmcapital.com/news/lfm-capital-completes-sale-of-medix)
in 2021. The newly-formed Demers Braun Crestline Medix (DBCM) then
[announced](https://www.demers-ambulances.com/press_release/demers-braun-
crestline-announces-the-acquisition-of-medix-specialty-vehicles/) that "more
than one in three ambulances in North America is built in a Demers
manufacturing facility." The numbers here are clearly estimates. Combining
DBCM's third of the market with REV Group's estimated market share means that
between three-quarters and almost all ambulances in North America are now
manufactured by one of the nine brands owned by these two groups. (DBCM was
[sold to yet another private equity firm in
2025](https://www.jbpoindexter.com/news/j-b-poindexter-co-inc-acquires-
ambulance-manufacturing-leader-demers-braun-crestline-medix/)).

In other words, these two private equity groups seem to have eliminated
independent ambulance manufacturing operations in North America.

REV Group and DBCM have faced real challenges, as every company did during the
pandemic and post-pandemic era. To increase manufacturing capacity, [Crestline
](https://crestlineambulances.com/us/crestline-coach-tackles-production-lead-
times-through-its-expansion-project/)opened a 30,000 square foot manufacturing
space, [Horton ](https://revgroup.com/rev-group-announces-expansion-
investment-in-horton-emergency-vehicles-to-increase-capacity/)opened a 20,000
square foot space, and [Medix ](https://www.ems1.com/medix-specialty-vehicles-
expands-paint-plant-to-improve-ambulance-lead-times)opened a 7000 square foot
space. But these investments have not restored the competitive dynamics of the
market. And there is a likely reason for that -- investors love backlogs.

In 2025, REV Group [reported ](https://investors.revgroup.com/investor-
releases/2025/12-10-2025-120033927)almost $4.4 billion in unfulfilled fire
truck and ambulance orders in their investor materials as a "highlight." While
executives have tried to blame delays on [semiconductor
shortages](https://www.ems1.com/ems-products/fleet-management/articles/when-
the-chips-are-down-ambulance-chassis-availability-now-at-crisis-levels-
fdggdvlHfQ9c5uTw/#:~:text=Typical%20ambulance%20production%20timeline%20and,Daimler%20Trucks%2DNorth%20and%20Navistar.)
and [limited chassis supply](https://www.jems.com/ems-operations/ground-
ambulance-operations/microchip-shortage-affecting-
ems/#:~:text=Ford%20supplies%20about%2070%25%20of,up%20with%20the%20demand%2C%20however.),
REV Group has touted its extreme backlog as a way to increase shareholder
value because it "[enables strong visibility into future net
sales.](https://investors.revgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/Rev-
IR/Annual%20Reports/rev-annual-report-2023.pdf)" And, indeed, the company's
stock price increased [640 percent](https://finance.yahoo.com/lookup/?s=REVG)
in the last five years.

The consolidation of ambulance production into the hands of two conglomerates
is one part of the problem, but there have also been two other changes in the
structure of this market. The first is that REV Group and DBCM may be seeking
to control the entire purchasing and aftermarket experience as well. Their
brands rely on networks of exclusive dealers that are licensed to sell their
ambulances on [state-by-state ](https://aev.com/dealer-locator/)or
[regional](https://hortonambulance.com/dealer-locator/) basis. By forcing
buyers to purchase ambulances from licensed dealers while eliminating
competition between them, the two dominant conglomerates appear to be enabling
their dealers to further raise ambulance prices.

As Damian Rice, a paramedic in Hancock County, Kentucky [noted
](https://www.hancockclarion.com/2022/09/14/hancock-fiscal-court-surprised-at-
cost-of-new-ambulance/)when comparing a price increase between a 2020
ambulance purchase and a 2022 ambulance purchase, "you have to go through a
dealer now," and "[w]ith the dealer mark-up, it raised the price
significantly." Rice continued "[j]ust from when we tried to do this bid back
in May, it's [_sic_] went up $60,000… he said they were seeing a 20 percent
increase, just on materials."

### Ford and the Chassis Shortage

The second change has to do with the platform on which ambulances are built.
An ambulance is essentially the body of a vehicle, known as a chassis, with a
bunch of construction on top. "It's kind of like taking a van and turning it
into an ambulance because it was cabinet work, electrical work, things of that
nature," said Scott Barnes, the founder of Wheeled Coach. The ambulance
producers buy those base chassis from major automakers like Dodge, Chevy,
Mercedes, and Ford. Ford alone [controls seventy
percent](https://ambulance.org/sp_product/ambulance-fleet-maintenance-tips-
for-weathering-the-chassis-shortage/) of the ambulance chassis
market.[1](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/feed#footnote-1)

Despite facing chassis shortages as early as
[2018](https://investors.revgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/Rev-IR/reports-and-
presentations/revg-ms-laguna-presentation.pdf) (which stabilized in
[2019](https://investors.revgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/Rev-IR/reports-and-
presentations/revg-stifel-conference-june-2019.pdf#page=16)) and Ford
predicting a production shortfall of 1.1 million ambulance chassis in 2021
[after a production halt,](https://ambulance.org/2021/05/19/microchip-
shortage-to-affect-ambulance-supply/) every private equity-owned ambulance
manufacturer continues to rely on the major automakers for chassis. This total
reliance continues despite [REV
Group](https://investors.revgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/Rev-IR/reports-and-
presentations/revg-ms-laguna-presentation.pdf#page=21) telling its investors
that chassis supply issues have lost the company up to $120 million in
incremental revenue. (We contacted a number of officials at Ford and asked
about chassis production, but no one responded.)

This chassis shortage and the industry's excessive reliance on Ford isn't a
result of some inherent feature of the industry; it's just a function of
whether REV Group and DBCM want to make the required capital investment from
the enormous profits they have earned over the past few years. Indeed, some of
the same companies REV Group and DBCM rolled up used to build ambulance
chassis. For example, in 2009, Spartan Motor Chassis (now called Spartan
Emergency Response)
[announced](https://www.fireengineering.com/firefighting/spartan-chassis-
announces/#:~:text=Share%20To:,bringing%20it%20to%20the%20market.) the first
orders, placed by then-independent Braun Ambulance, of its FurionRT ambulance
chassis, which it sold through its subsidiary Road Rescue. Though the
company's time as an ambulance chassis supplier [ended a year
later](https://americanindustrial.com/allied-specialty-vehicles-inc-announces-
the-acquisition-of-road-rescue/) after it sold Road Rescue to Allied Specialty
Vehicles (AIP's roll-up vehicle for this sector in the early 2010s, which it
transformed into REV Group around 2015), this effort shows it is possible for
these companies to manufacture chassis internally. REV's decision not to do so
despite acquiring Spartan in 2020 is indicative of a dominant market position
that allows the company to spend just [one percent of its
revenue](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/17/us/fire-engines-shortage-private-
equity.html) on capital investments in buildings and equipment, even as it
faces a several billion-dollar backlog of unfulfilled orders. Indeed, one
reason Terex
[bought](https://s203.q4cdn.com/676879669/files/doc_financials/2025/q4/Terex-Q4-25-Presentation-
Final.pdf) Rev Group is because of its "low capital intensity," AKA the fact
it doesn't need to invest into more production.

Since 2020, REV Group has
[focused](https://acrobat.adobe.com/id/urn:aaid:sc:US:5826308f-d5c8-4eb5-8c06-8e90649e9c82)
Spartan primarily on supplying [fire apparatus
chassis](https://spartaner.com/fire-trucks/) to its own fire truck brands and
limited fire chassis sales to outside[ buyers who
agree](https://forums.firehouse.com/forum/emergency-vehicles-
operation/apparatus-innovation/113972-was-spartan-erv-a-good-move-for-spartan)
not to make, or plan to make, their own chassis. Current President of REV Fire
Group and REV Specialty Group Mike Virnig led this strategy in his prior role
as [Spartan's Director of North American
Sales](https://www.facebook.com/SpartanEmergencyResponse/photos/mike-virnig-
director-of-north-american-sales-at-spartan-motors-had-the-honor-
of-/1252242464788694/) before joining REV Group and pushing to acquire
Spartan. In following this strategy, REV Group has boasted to investors that
it has been able to "[drive margin improvement
actions](https://investors.revgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/Rev-IR/reports-and-
presentations/rev-group-investor-day-v18.pdf#page=35)" while reducing[ its
manufacturing production capacity by a
third](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/17/us/fire-engines-shortage-private-
equity.html).

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EUBD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4a25cdfe-f846-453b-af9a-618a5fa77bc3_692x644.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EUBD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4a25cdfe-f846-453b-af9a-618a5fa77bc3_692x644.png)

Soon after REV Group went public, its CEO at the time, Tim Sullivan, told
shareholders he expected to more than double the profit margins of the
companies REV acquired from the historic norm of four or five percent to more
than ten percent in short order. This followed a 2018 shareholder call where
he declared "[w]e like backlog, _**we love backlog. " **_And indeed, REV
Group's choices in the face of exploding order backlogs -- such as not even
attempting to produce its own ambulance chassis despite owning companies that
had previously done so -- have proven extremely lucrative. REV Group's
Adjusted EBITDA for its Specialty Vehicles division -- the best measure of REV
Group's "operating fundamentals," according to its management's SEC reports --
has soared dramatically in recent years, increasing by $92.5 million (or
149.2%) from 2023 to 2024, and by an additional $89.7 million (or 65.5%) from
2024 to 2025.

To cope with cost increases and production delays, towns are increasingly
choosing remounts, replacing only the ambulance chassis rather than purchasing
an entirely new vehicle. Despite the existing chassis shortage, turnaround
times for remounts are far shorter because manufacturing a new ambulance
requires synchronized production of a new chassis and a new patient module
(interior of an ambulance),[ securing a non-customized chassis
](https://crestlineambulances.com/ca/a-new-era-for-ambulance-remount-
standards-a-certified-program-redefining-
quality/#:~:text=Addressing%20Pandemic%20Challenges%20and%20Rising,seamlessly%20integrate%20into%20the%20fleet.)to
mount the module on allows for towns to bypass [microchip
shortages](https://www.denver7.com/news/national/the-global-chip-shortage-is-
causing-problems-for-first-
responders#:~:text=%E2%80%9CThe%20microchip%20to%20what%2C%20I,ambulance%2C%22%20Van%20Arnam%20said.)
and other production issues plaguing the ambulance manufacturing market. Towns
looking to save money decide to replace the chassis alone because the chassis
comprises [a significant percentage
](https://www.scriptype.com/2022/07/23/council-approves-purchase-of-new-
ambulance-chassis/)of the [entire ambulance](https://www.demers-
ambulances.com/ambulance-remounts-maximizing-savings-without-compromising-
quality/#:~:text=Given%20that%20the%20chassis%20typically,a%20modern%20and%20reliable%20fleet.)
purchase price, and replacing the chassis by itself enables [meaningful cost
savings.](https://www.plaintalk.net/local_news/article_c6e644ae-b8be-11e6-8c33-7fc181c054f1.html)

This trend has been brought on by necessity, as seen by Coalinga, California's
[decision
](https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___https:/coalinga.novusagenda.com/AgendaPublic/CoverSheet.aspx?ItemID=5821&MeetingID=617___.YzJ1OmFlbHBlY29ub21pY2xpYmVydGllczpjOm86M2YyNGQwZGMwNTE2M2ZlNGZhOWRmNzRhYWI3MjBlMDc6NzphNTc4OjFhMmJiMjk3NWY1OTU1YTg3MTZiYmI1MzVjNjY5ZGIzNmI0NmUwMWFiNzU5YjUzNTQ3ZTMzNDMzMjJlMmFmMWQ6cDpUOkY)this
past April. Rather than paying $445,000 for a new ambulance to arrive in two
years, replacing the chassis alone saved $200,000, and ensured the ambulance
would be in service in the next eight months. While this approach is cost and
time-effective, even the chassis market seems to changed. Just five years ago,
Spartanburg, South Carolina [replaced its chassis
](https://emsrig.com/2021/02/03/old-ambulance-just-replace-the-chassis/)for
less than half what it cost Coalinga to do so in 2025.

Record wait times, backlogs, and price increases were not inevitable. Modern
ambulances have been manufactured for [more than a
century](https://www.nationalmuseum.af.mil/Visit/Museum-Exhibits/Fact-
Sheets/Display/Article/197425/ford-model-t-ambulance/). Up through the first
decade of this century, delivery times remained stable in the 120-day range,
and price increases were modest. The change in market structure removed any
notion of cost or delivery certainty, leaving towns and cities across the
country with no choice but to pay an ever-increasing premium for a vehicle
that will most likely only be ready years in the future.

We do not have to accept this situation as our new normal. As recent
congressional hearings into "[America's Fire Apparatus
Crisis](https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/subcommittees/dmdcc/hearings/sounding-
the-alarm-americas-fire-apparatus-crisis/)" made clear, we are not powerless
to address markets. There are now more [than a
dozen](https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/subcommittees/dmdcc/hearings/sounding-the-
alarm-americas-fire-apparatus-crisis/) antitrust cases against the fire truck
oligopoly, many of which are explicitly seeking to reverse the serial
acquisitions by REV Group that consolidated that industry. Overall, existing
law equips lawmakers, federal agencies, cities, and state Attorneys General
with tools to investigate and break-up what appears to be a PE-created duopoly
in ambulance manufacturing.

In 1988, Ford launched what is now known as its [Upfitter
](https://www.fromtheroad.ford.com/img/en/home)program to "offer guidelines to
vehicle converters over key requirements for engineering, manufacturing,
quality and process control" in converting Ford chassis for other uses. GM has
a similar program called [GM Envolve](https://www.gmenvolve.com/fleet/upfit-
applications), while Mercedes' is called[ eXpert
Upfitter](https://www.mbvans.com/en/upfitter/apply). Each of these companies
says that Upfitter certification is not required for a downstream manufacturer
to be allowed to build an ambulance using their chassis. However, all major
ambulance manufacturing brands have had these Upfitter certifications for
years, and they [rely on them](https://www.jems.com/industry-news/braun-
ambulances-earns-prestigious-ford-pro-upfitter-qualified-status/) for
marketing and quality assurance operations. Although from a cursory glance it
does not seem like these Upfitter programs are designed to "lock" ambulance
brands into continuing to use the major automakers for chassis, they may give
automakers some leverage over ambulance manufacturers which is susceptible to
abuse.
